Revision 0: April 4, 2012 Country of Publication: India mṛgendravṛttidīpikā (The Lamp on the Commentary on the Mṛgendra)
The *Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā*: A Commentary on the *Mṛgendravṛtti* composed by Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇakaṇṭha.
I pay homage to that Supreme Lord, the ordainer of all knowledge, whose powers in the form of gnosis and action bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. [From] the *Mṛgendravṛtti*.

We shall clarify the intended meaning—which is not contradicted by scripture, logic, or tradition—as established by the venerable Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha. Regarding that meaning which the author of the commentary himself understands clearly in this Śaiva scripture, there is indeed nothing further to be said; for what has been stated by him is sufficient.
Nevertheless, out of fear of prolixity, some points that were either not mentioned or only vaguely indicated have now been stated by me, in accordance with scripture and reasoning.

O Rāmakaṇṭha, O Mahākaṇṭha, follower of the feet of Kaṇṭhīrava! I, who am not a mere sophist, do not fear the roars of the elephants [of opposing arguments]. In this regard, first, with the first half-verse, he pays homage to the nine Tāraka-gurus—the Lord and his disciples—who are the authors of the scripture and the source of its materials, for the sake of the proper instruction of disciples and the unimpeded completion of the treatise; with the second half-verse, however, he pledges to provide an exposition of the scripture. [He salutes] the Half-moon.

Because it illuminates like the moon and because it bestows delight, the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) alone is thus called the digit of the moon (*candra-kalā*). That very [power] is the crest-ornament (*cūḍābhūṣaṇa*) of Him of whom it is revealed in scripture that "the mind is the digit of the moon of knowledge. The two feet (*caraṇau*) of that Supreme Lord are His powers of knowledge and action; they are so called because "one moves (*caryate*) by them," meaning one goes, knows, and acts, and because "one is moved (*caryate*) by them," meaning one proceeds, practices, and performs [actions]. These two powers serve as the instruments for the composition of the scriptures, as he will state later: "The instrument is not other than power."

Because they possess the nature of blooming and are stainless, these two are "lotuses" (*abja*). Their "pair" (*yuga*) is their collective form; although they are one in essence as Power (*śakti*), they are called a "pair" through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), intended to distinguish them by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and its effect (*kārya*). Having bowed with body, speech, and mind—having become prostrate before Vāgīśvarī, who is the material cause of the scripture, whose nature is Great Māyā, who abides as the consort, and whose essential form is Supreme Knowledge—as it is stated in the venerable *Pauṣkara*:
The supreme Vāgīśvarī-vidyā is known as Mahāmāyā.
As he will state [later]: "From Śakti, the Nāda arises," and so forth; likewise, [it pertains to] the Gaṇas, the Vidyeśvaras, the Vidyās, and the lower Mantreśvaras.

Having bowed to Paramaśiva, the Lord of the hosts of bound souls (*paśu*) and the author of this scripture—first, because he is the efficient cause (*kartṛ*) of the act of composition; second, because even an agent requires an instrument (*karaṇa*), thus taking up the instrument first; and third, because an instrument itself requires a material cause (*upādāna*), one subsequently sets forth the material cause and the sequence [of transmission] in due order: the gurus Ananta, Śrīkaṇṭha, Śakra, Bharadvāja, Hārīta, and others who brought down the Tantras.

Having prostrated before the lineage of gurus, he bows to the glorious *Mṛgendra* for its ultimate meaning. By this, he demonstrates the authority of the scripture through its being composed by the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), and his own status as one who has received it through an unbroken tradition. "In brief" means concisely, according to his intellect and according to his understanding. If that is so, then even Brahmā would be able to fully comprehend the scripture of the Supreme Lord; if this were the case—

One who speaks something merely according to their own fancy would be nothing more than a mere fool; therefore, he says: "according to tradition" (*yathāgama*) means by not transgressing scripture and inference.

The meaning is that because the subject matter is both pure and profound, this [text] is to be explained by way of its specific characteristics during the process of exposition; the reason for this is its purity, and thus it must be explained.
Because he possesses the glorious sovereignty over all, the Supreme Lord is "Vishva"; that scripture in which He exists as the author is "Shrimad. And this...

Now, as for the *Mṛgendra*: it is true that among the eighteen distinct scriptures (*śāstras*), there is nothing at all known by the name *Mṛgendra*. For this very reason, this scripture of knowledge (*jñāna-śāstra*) called *Kāmika* is termed *Mṛgendra* because it was heard by Śakra in the form of Mṛgendra. As he will state in the conclusion:
"This *Kāmika* knowledge has been obtained by me from the Supreme Lord," and likewise: "And this knowledge is supremely secret."

"Whatever is well-nourished throughout the three worlds, because of his lion-like form, he is the 'Lord of Beasts' (mṛgendra), and he is 'Surabhi' (the Auspicious One)"; thus, "I shall manifest"—that is, I shall reveal—"his ultimate meaning according to its true nature. With this second verse, [the author] addresses both types of commentators: those who, though not relevant to the context, prattle on excessively, and those who, considering themselves clever, neglect the meaning of the text that is to be explained under the pretext that it is already clear.

He objects: by the second [verse], indicating the correctness of his own explanation, he states the definition of a correct explanation in three verses beginning with "sākṣāt" (directly), and he also declares the reason for engaging in the explanation of the tradition of the treatise. The intention is that, just as in the case of study, hearing, and so forth, the cause for engaging even in the explanation of the treatise is solely by the command of the guru; as it was said by the Teachers: "Also because of approaching the guru."

"In all matters, one must proceed solely according to the words of the Guru"—this is the *Mṛgendra-śāstra*. By the passage beginning with "kimapīti" (whatever it may be), it resolves what has been left unsaid, what was poorly said, and what is doubtful; and by the phrase "doṣā rātri-guṇa-viparyayāśca" (faults, nights, qualities, and their reversals), it states that they should proceed with this very measure of internal consistency. With the words "ataḥ param" (beyond this), he demonstrates the nature of the scripture (*śāstra*).
Now, with the words beginning "Then, without beginning" (*athānādi*), he states the purpose of the introductory chapter (*upodghāta-paṭala*).

With the words beginning "That which," they say: "They declare the introduction to be for the sake of accomplishing the subject at hand. He provides the prelude to the introductory chapter with the words beginning "In former times...

and ending with "by those who have received initiation. The meaning is that there is no authority over the worlds for those who have not been initiated. The section beginning with "the upward stream" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) constitutes the nature of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

The *Navāma*, and so forth, is known by the name *Mṛgendrottara* because it was spoken to Mṛgendra; thus it is called the *Mṛgendrottara*, but it is not identical to the *Mṛgendra* alone, due to its connection with the four sections beginning with Jñāna. Regarding the statement that [the scriptures] are "endowed with the qualities of disciples," they say: "One who is free from affliction, capable, and learned is not excluded by the scripture and is made to act within the Tantra. Because of the inclusion of [the passage] beginning with "from the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvarāt*), Bhāradvāja is the first to be saluted at the beginning of the commentary and is the Guru.
The statement "Hārīta, the disciple of Hārīta," and so forth, means that the very word of Hārīta was experienced by his disciples and others. A *vrata* is a scriptural performance;

thus, by way of general and specific [definition], the scripture (*śāstra*) is established. As it is said in the venerable *Bhārgava*: "One should not transgress the conduct of the castes and stages of life even in thought. Whosoever, abiding in a particular stage of life (*āśrama*), has received initiation into the nature of Śiva, he should remain steadfast in that very stage."

"One should protect the Śivadharma"—thus it is stated even in the venerable *Svāyambhuva*. Those who abide by the path of Brahmā’s world, having been initiated into the worldly conduct (*laukika-ācāra*), should not transgress it;
they should act accordingly. By the word "Hara" in such passages as "He removes the bonds from the bound souls (*paśu*)," the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha, the disciple of Ananta, is meant.
He states the reason for this right here: "because [he is] the source of the word 'Indra'. The meaning is that he holds authority over the interior of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). This very point...

He introduces the elaboration with "Why? and so forth, and answers it with "Because" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "Hara and the others have come to death," he states that the word "Indra" is also an elliptical designation for Bharadvāja and the rest, saying "in the order beginning with Indra. He explains the *Jñānapāda* (Knowledge Section) with the words "That by which one knows," and so forth.

Here, by the word "Vidyā" (Knowledge), what is denoted by the *Vidyāpāda*—namely, the Lord and the others below—is understood; for [liberation] occurs through the manifestation of Śiva-nature in one who is graced by that.

Because omniscience is manifested in the case of the Vidyeśvaras and others solely through the grace of Śiva—as he will state: "At the outset, for the sake of those individual souls (*aṇu*) who are fit, He creates [the Lord] joined with the powers such as Vāmā and so forth, accompanied by the retinue of seventy million"—it follows that the term "Lord" (*Īśa*) has its primary application to Him alone. As for the phrase "by His own independence" and so on: although Ananta and the others are omniscient, they act as the causes of creation and so forth only through His impulsion; therefore, [He is the Lord] even in comparison to them.

The meaning is that the agency [of Bharadvāja] is inferior. Anticipating the objection that the word "ṛṣi" is redundant given that the seerhood of Bharadvāja is already well-known, he offers a rebuttal:

by including the phrase "from the connection with the movement of lightning and so forth," both the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) are understood here for the sake of revealing the relationship [between the work and its subject]. He tells a story, beginning with "Once upon a time... and so forth; "viharaṇa-hevākīna" means one who is addicted to play, [and thus] entirely [immersed in it].

The phrase "the end of suffering has arisen for him" means that because he is the cause of all suffering, the end—the disappearance—of all the impurities of suffering has arisen; at that very moment, by virtue of the ripening of those impurities, his initiation into liberation (nirvāṇa-dīkṣā) was accomplished, preceded by the descent of grace (śaktipāta).

Precisely because of this qualification, the *Śrīmat Kāmika*—the scripture whose nature is that of the Supreme Lord—was taught to him; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. To clarify the relationship [between the teacher and the teaching], he says "the relationship," and so forth. "The supreme and so on" means: the supreme (*para*), the great intermediate (*mahānantarāla*), the divine (*divya*), and those beginning with the divine (*divyādi*). He demonstrates these very [categories] with the words "for instance," and so forth, stating that it is "divided into five streams. This very work is of the nature of the Siddhānta, because it encompasses the five mantras and because it expounds the five-fold cosmic act (*pañcakṛtya*).

Furthermore, because it is manifested as the body of Śiva consisting of the five mantras, it is called the "five-fold stream" (*pañcasrotas*). Even the ninefold and other [streams] are so designated because they perform the work of Śiva. But how is it that these too are well-known in some places as being Śaiva? It is by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), since they were composed by other souls presided over by Śiva. If this is so, then since the Supreme Lord is bodiless, the teaching of the scriptures would be untenable; [but this is not so], for it is not like the creation of the world and so forth.

11) Since the Vidyeśvaras and others are made aware of the scriptures by mere volition (*saṃkalpa*) alone, he says "graced by his own will" and so forth. Now, it is heard that the *Kāmika* and other divisions of Śiva were taught to Praṇava and the rest; how then can there be instruction for the Vidyeśvaras? To this, he says:
"Immediately after the awakening of the eight Vidyeśvaras"—thus first comes the instruction for the Vidyeśvaras, and afterwards for Praṇava and the others.

"From them [it came] to Umāpati"; immediately after them, from the venerable Ananta, comes the attainment of Śrīkaṇṭha, since he is well known as the disciple of Sūkṣma and the others. And it is said in the venerable Raurava: "Ananteśa is the cause of the universe, the supreme Guru; by him were the instructions spoken."
"To the great-souled Śrīkaṇṭha"—thus, there is a supreme relationship between Śiva and Ananta; a great [relationship] between Ananta and Śrīkaṇṭha;

an intermediate [relationship] between Śrīkaṇṭha and Śakra; [an intermediate one] between Śakra and Bhāradvāja; and from that, a divine [one] for Bhāradvāja and Hārīta, followed by a non-divine [one] for the disciples.

Regarding knowledge (*jñāna*), action (*kriyā*), yoga, and conduct (*caryā*): here, by the word "knowledge," the Lord (*pati*), the bound soul (*paśu*), and the fetters (*pāśa*) are meant to be understood; and the purpose here is realization (*jñapti*).

This very relationship, characterized as the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*), is indicated here. Thus, because both [the author and the knower] possess the form of Indra, and because they function as the agent and the indicator respectively, there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itarētarāśraya*) due to their distinct roles. He clarifies this very point through an illustration with the words "Just as someone," and so forth.
He connects the second sūtra with the words "Thus, in this way," and so forth, because the hermitages of Nārāyaṇa are manifold.

In response to the inquiry "In what [place]?", he says: "Of the hermitages of Badarī. He explains the term *dvija* (twice-born) with the words "of Bharadvāja and others," and so forth. Regarding what was stated—that the first birth is of Māyā, and from that [birth] follows the subsequent one—how is it that Bharadvāja and the others were already initiated prior to their direct realization of Indra? It is not so; rather, at the time of Hārīta’s instruction, they were like those described in the Sūtra as "twice-born" in the manner of the Smṛtis.

As Devala has said: "When a child has been consecrated by his parents through the *garbhādhāna* and other rites, he becomes eligible for the *upanayana* in the eighth year from conception; in that regard, the teacher (*upādhyāya*), the father, the mother, and the *gāyatrī* [are the authorities]. Even though thus initiated, who would be a twice-born (*dvija*)? Because of the lack of eligibility to hear the primary knowledge (*ādidhī-śravaṇa*). By the inclusion of the word "primary" (*ādi*), the *mantras* are also implied. As it is stated in the venerable *Kālottara*: "The *mantra-tantra* has been proclaimed by you"—thus, even regarding the hearing of the *mantra-tantra*.

The qualification belongs exclusively to those who have been initiated, as it is stated in the venerable *Varāha*: "One who is initiated shall be qualified for worship in the appropriate places and so forth," and he will further state in the section on study:
"Standing upon purified ground, [the teacher] is free from hearing [the scriptures] of the *paśus*. As for what was said regarding the scriptural mention of transgression in the venerable *Raurava*:
"From the violation of the Command (*ājñā*), one is declared to be a flesh-eater (*kravyāda*) for a hundred years. Or else, by the word "twice-born" (*dvija*), their...

The pervasion of the state of being twice-born (*dvijatva*) is proclaimed as an excellence through the conjunction with knowledge, just as it is through the fruit [of action]. Even in the absence of self-knowledge regarding one's own self and so forth, because omniscience is observed, the power of those very means of knowledge that perceive the bondage within bondage belongs to Śiva—the knower of the means for its eradication—by virtue of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). Thus, it results in the worship of Śiva characterized by the removal of impurity (*pariṇatamala*), by virtue of the descent of power.

That which was stated in the venerable *Kiraṇa* as being of the nature of the *Śivadharmas* and so forth—namely, that when a [karmic] action has been performed, by the force of the passage of time, there occurs a descent of the exceedingly intense power (*tīvra-śakti*)—is also stated in the venerable *Svāyaṃbhuva*: "That power, having reached the soul (*puruṣa*), through its final descent, causes its impurity (*mala*), the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), to flow away; when that [impurity] is exhausted, supreme liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) follows for it."

15) In this context, regarding the reading *buddhālunī*, the meaning is *śivaśuddhālunī*. He stated [this] with the intention that he expressed the meaning of each word individually, speaking according to the Mīmāṃsaka perspective; by the word *codanā* here, injunctions and prohibitions (*vidhi-niṣedha*) are denoted, as he says in the passage beginning with *codanā*.

Because the authority of injunctive sentences (*codanāvākya*) is admitted only with respect to an object that is to be accomplished (*kārya*), it is not [authoritative] regarding mere cognition (*buddhi*). Since [injunctions] such as "one should sprinkle" (*bindet*) function as motivators by having the purpose of establishing a mere cognition, how can there be the presentation [of them] as "verbal expression" (*vacana*)? True; the meaning of an injunction is indeed mere cognition alone;

however, it impels a person only when it depends upon a productive activity (*bhāvanā*). This is the meaning: when it is said, "One should do this," and there arises an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to what, by what means, and in what manner, [it is understood that] "this [is to be done] by this [means]..."

The injunctive force belongs to the sentence itself in the form "one should act thus," as they say: "A suffix, complete and capable through its requirements such as 'what' and so forth, effects the injunction. Here, by the word *dharma*, a quality of the intellect (*buddhi-guṇa*) consisting of an abstract suffix (*bhāva-pratyaya*) is not intended, because that is unacceptable to the Mīmāṃsakas; nor is it the nature of an action (*bhāva-svabhāva*), because that is something to be produced (*kārya*); nor is it the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) called *apūrva*, because that arises only after the performance [of the rite]. Rather—

He says that it consists precisely in the performance of sacrifices and so forth; therefore, [the Veda] is its self and is called "protection" (*varma*), for it is not something that is merely performed. Since *codanā* (injunction) alone is the authority regarding *dharma*, even though *dharma*—which consists of performance—is perceptible, its result known as "the unseen" (*apūrva*) produced by that, as well as heaven and the like, and the relationship between them, are beyond the senses. Consequently, the validity of means of knowledge such as perception does not apply there. If this is so...

The authority of the tantras is *codanā*; therefore, he says that *codanā* alone is the authority. Because *codanā* is eternal, it is free from defects such as deception on the part of an author; thus, its authority consists in its being a means of making known objects through the senses.

It is indeed unavoidable that they have stated: "A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which makes known an object not yet apprehended. By the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*), it excludes the possibility of the injunction (*codanā*) not being a means of valid cognition. However, by the restriction (*evakāra*) "the injunction alone," it excludes the possibility of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means being means of valid cognition. [The phrase] "the non-aggregation of the result" [is used]; but surely, in some cases such as the *putreṣṭi* sacrifice, a discrepancy regarding the result is observed. How then can the result...?

"Not [a means] for establishing an invalid result. He introduces the subsequent sūtra with the words "it has little purpose" (*phalaprāyam ityalpaprayojanam*), beginning with "in this way" (*ityevam*) and "this which has been stated by us" (*yo'yam asmābhiḥ*).
The meaning is: let the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) alone be the authority (*pramāṇa*) regarding dharma, and we too shall perform only that dharma which is enjoined. (p.

"‘For the sake of accomplishing what is desired’—this establishes that their desired goal, such as the cessation of impurity (*mala*), is indeed the nature of the injunction (*codanā*) and the very essence of *dharma*. To this effect, he says ‘for thus,’ and so forth. It was stated that the injunctive sentence alone is the instigator; however, one might object: ‘We do not accept every instigating sentence as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but rather only the injunction in the form of revealed scripture (*śruti*). To this he replies: ‘Even granting [that it is scripture], there is delusion,’ and so on, followed by ‘again,’ and so forth. Due to the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), there arises a doubt regarding the will of the Lord (*īśvara*)."

The meaning is that the existence of those [entities] is revealed through the destruction of erroneous cognition (*viparyaya-jñāna*) and through certainties (*niścaya*); however, one should not explain "great delusion" (*mahāmoha*) here as being the impurity (*mala*), because it has already been stated that its exhaustion occurs through initiation (*dīkṣā*) alone. Having said this, he explains the sūtra beginning with "even so," etc., and explains "the supreme state" (*paraṃ bhāvam*) as "the excellence of devotion to Him. The fitness for the descent of power (*śaktipāta-yogyatā*) itself is "being established in that" (*tanniṣṭhatvam*); it is characterized by the penetration of the fitness for devotion.

A specific type of knowledge is what was stated: "Another [form] is said to be characterized by the penetration of fitness (yogyatāveśa), which is designated as devotion (bhakti) and arises from a portion of supreme wisdom.

For this very reason, since the transformation of their impurities has now been accomplished and the power of the Supreme Lord exists as the sign of the descent of grace (śaktipāta), I shall once again examine them through the perspective of a Mīmāṃsaka in order to ascertain the degree of that excellence. Thus he spoke most excellently.

Having thus stated that [the deity] does not have the nature of a manifestation, he says: "The fruit comes from the performance of the ritual alone, not from the deity. This is because the specific deities intended to be denoted by words such as Rudra and Īśa are not established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, it is impossible to grasp a relationship with them. Consequently, they are not established even by scripture (*āgama*), precisely because no relationship can be grasped therein. Furthermore, since their establishment would involve mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), they remain unestablished. Thus, even in cases such as "one should offer a *caru* oblation to Rudra," [the deity] remains to be taught.

Since it is distinguished as a constituent part of a specific ritual action (*karmāṅga*), that very word "deity" (*devatā-śabda*) is what is perceived; thus, he will state here as well that the fruit arises from the action itself and not from the deity, and that there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish that [position] which is contradicted by the Bhāṣya.
Furthermore, even if one were to admit that [the deity] is something other than the word, the specific deity you intend would still not be established; thus he says, "And not here," and so forth.

The intention is that even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others are heard of as being subject to destruction by the Lord of the Universe (*viśveśi*). Nor is such an admission logical; thus he says, "That is established," meaning it is certain. He states the connection to the sūtra beginning with "other than sound" (*śabdetara*) and so forth: "In this way, by positive concomitance" (*anvayena*) and so forth; "of the nature of experience" (*anubhavarūpa*) and so forth; because no other form besides having a body or not having a body is possible; and "of both forms" (*ubhayarūpa*) and so forth—it is that very same thing.

By stating "existence, non-existence, etc.," he declares that the doctrine of manifoldness (*anekāntavāda*) is untenable. Regarding the phrase "the two positions of the reversed nature of existence" and so forth:

faults are conceivable for both positions—namely, having a physical form and not having a physical form—such as being limited in knowledge and being an ineffective agent. Since these [faults] apply to both of them here, one might generally establish the mere word "deity" regarding the divinity, yet [this does not prove] the actual existence of its specific instance known as Īśvara.

He says "na kila" and so forth to state that the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) does not establish that [absence], and so on. In that regard, he first states that God is not an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*) by saying "by being beyond the senses" (*parokṣatvena*) and so forth, and "for indeed" (*na hi*) and so forth.
As they have said: "When there is contact with an existing object, the arising of cognition through the sense organs is the cause of perception, because it is the apprehension of what is present."

With the words "Now," and so forth, [the author] raises an objection regarding the validity of yogic perception as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and refutes it with the words "That is not so," and so forth. [He explains: "Because there is a lack of evidence; indeed, even the existence of a yogin is not established, much less that there exists an inference based on the presence of his perception. To this, he objects with the words "But surely," and so forth.
This is stated by accepting the very body of Īśvara according to the Paurāṇika school, since Bharadvāja and others have not mastered the treatises on established tenets (*siddhānta*).

Regarding that, [the author] states the sublation of that [position] with "If this were so," and so forth. Therein, he states the existence of the cause—the whole (*avayavin*)—with "That whole," and so forth.

With "Of atoms, the sense faculties, etc.," he states what is accepted by you; that is to say, by those like you who maintain the doctrine of atoms, such as the Sāṃkhyas and others. If it is argued, "In that case, they would not have the nature of being effects," [the response is: "Atoms are eternal substances devoid of parts."
One could also say, "like yourself," and so forth; for this very reason, since the world's status as an effect is not established, its being preceded by a creator is also refuted.

Now, having provisionally accepted the world's status as an effect, he states the refutation with the words beginning with "furthermore" (*kiñca*). To explain that [the reason] is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*), he raises an objection with the words beginning with "if it is said" (*athocyate*). Then, he states that the answer is given by this portion of the sūtra with the words beginning with "this very thing" (*etadeva*).

"Parāṇeti," "hāsādi," and "gītam"—these are examples of injunctive statements (*pravartaka-vākya*) even in the Śruti, when intended in a general sense. However, with the intention of specifying particular cases, he explains that both types of statements are established otherwise (*tadanyathā-siddha*), in order to refute them. The underlying intent is that the authority of injunctions (*codanā*) lies solely in matters that are to be accomplished (*kārya*). He demonstrates this very point with the words "atra hi" and so forth, regarding the sentences such as *arthavāda* found within the Vedas.

Since there would otherwise follow the consequence [of these] being independent means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*), he says "In the Śruti," and so forth. Now, because comparison (*upamāna*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) are included within inference (*anumāna*), and because non-existence (*abhāva*) and possibility (*sambhava*) are included within perception (*pratyakṣa*), setting those aside, [the author states] that "only these [six] are authoritative according to worldly convention" (p.

To explain this according to the view of the Paurāṇikas, [the author] anticipates the objection that its lack of authority is established, saying: "Now, [it is] established for all the world," and so forth; the meaning is that he states what has already been said. He explains that very fragment of the Sūtra beginning with "not appropriate because of the limitlessness" (*aparyāptatvāt*); the sense is that its authority is not possible at all, because of the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). [The opponent] objects: "But no deviation is seen in that which is set forth by a reliable person (*āpta*)."

Regarding the passage beginning with *atha* and so forth, he states the refutation here as well, starting with *tarhi* and so forth. As for the scripture (*āgama*), this very same fault has been stated. Furthermore, from what source is the authority established for the reliability (*prāmāṇya*) of those speakers or of their respective statements? He says, beginning with *pratyayitaśca* and so forth. Regarding the phrase *tasya*, it refers to the author of the scripture. Now, is there not the *Saṃhitā* of the Vedas called *Raudrī*, which is said to have Rudra as its deity? To this he replies with the passage beginning *nityatve tu* and so forth. And this has already been stated previously. Thus ends the aphorism beginning with *anīśa*.

"He causes [the meaning] to descend" refers to the statement of Śakra and so forth; because of its substantiality (*sāravatva*) and weightiness (*gurutva*), there is substantiality in the Buddha. Because of its subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*), there is graspability (*grāhitva*) and weightiness, which means stability and the grasping of the object to be grasped. Regarding the phrase "not [as] a living being" (*na jīva*) and so forth, he states the connection of the Sūtra with the words "therefore" (*tatas tu*) and so forth. Herein lies the intention of the proponents of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*): if it were accepted that the deity is merely sound (*śabdamātra*), then in such passages as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," [the following would apply].

Even a result such as heaven, because it is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), would consist of the word alone; however, if it is argued that the word "heaven" denotes a specific object as a result because it is well-known from sources such as the Purāṇas and Itihāsas, then that is the same in this case as well, and thus the deity is established as being other than the word. And therefore, since [the deity] is other than the word...
